results.text:
Introduction

A lot of trauma healing gets talked about as if the main thing is going back into painful memories. But the body was there too, and it can keep bracing, collapsing, freezing, disconnecting, looking for danger, or flooding long after the danger itself is over.

So I don't think deeper is automatically better. Before going after the trauma itself, I want to know whether I can stay present enough to do anything useful with it. Can I stop if I need to? Can I come back to ordinary life afterward? This matters especially with complex or developmental trauma, where the nervous system may already have a very easy time getting overwhelmed.

That is why I'm putting Somatic Experiencing, trauma-sensitive yoga, EFT, shaking, Brainspotting, EMDR, and cognitive integration on the same loose map. They don't all do the same job. Some are therapies, some are things you can use alongside therapy, and some are experiential practices that seem to help particular people even though the research behind them is much thinner.

The rough movement I have in mind is safety and regulation first, then releasing some of the stress and survival responses that keep accumulating, then deeper processing when you can actually tolerate going there. It is a rough map, not a universal recipe.

All of this can also prepare the ground for deeper inner-child therapy. Sometimes making the body a little easier to live in changes how much old material you can approach without simply getting swallowed by it.
